extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or advanced high-school students studying elementary number theory and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapter on the natural numbers and basic number theory, covering induction, sums and progressions, binomial theorem, primes, congruences, and related theorems and conjectures. Aimed at learning methods of proof and fundamental results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a sequence of propositions A1, A2, A3, ... show (a) that if Ar is true then Ar+1 follows, and (b) that the first proposition A1 is true; then all Ai are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This logical principle rests on the fact that after any integer r there is a next r+1 and that any desired integer n may be reached by finitely many such steps. Use repeated application to prove A2, A3, ... It is fundamental and accepted as a basic principle of mathematical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care when applying induction (base case and implication must hold)
rubrics_metrics.description: In using induction one must always be sure that conditions (a) and (b) are really satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive arguments are sometimes indicated casually by 'etc.' in elementary instruction, but explicit checking is indispensable in subtle proofs. Neglecting the base case or the truth-transfer step can lead to absurdities (illustrated by a fallacious 'proof' that any two positive integers are equal). Induction verifies statements but does not discover hypotheses; it is a verification method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized induction (starting index a)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence A_a, A_{a+1}, A_{a+2}, ... is given (a some positive integer), and for every r >= a the truth of A_{r+1} follows from A_r, and A_a is known true, then A_n is true for all n >= a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the same reasoning as ordinary induction, replacing the sequence 1,2,3,... by a,a+1,a+2,... Allows strengthening certain inequalities by eliminating equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the smallest integer (well-ordering principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-empty set C of positive integers has a smallest member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is closely related to induction and can be used to prove the principle of mathematical induction as a theorem: assume some A_n is false, let C be set of n for which A_n is false, use smallest element p>1 and derive contradiction. Note it does not hold for sets of non-integers (e.g., positive fractions have no smallest member).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of first n integers formula (arithmetical progression special case)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction: base case A1 (1 = 1) holds; assume A_r: 1+...+r = r(r+1)/2, add (r+1) to both sides to get A_{r+1}. Also can be derived by pairing terms S_n = 1 + 2 + ... + n and reverse-order sum to get n(n+1)/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of an arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from the special case (a=0,d=1) and linearity: separate constant and arithmetic parts; can be shown by induction using the previous sum formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of a finite geometric progression
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction: verify base case n=1, assume formula for n=r and manipulate to obtain case r+1. Note the formula is meaningless for q=1 in this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality (1 + p)^n > 1 + n p for p > -1 and integer n >= 1
rubrics_metrics.description: For every number p > -1 and positive integer n, (1 + p)^n > 1 + n p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: assume (1+p)^r > 1 + r p, multiply both sides by (1+p) > 0, drop the positive rp^2 term to get (1+p)^{r+1} > 1 + (r+1)p. The restriction p > -1 is essential because if p < -1 then 1+p is negative and multiplying inequalities reverses sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle (coefficients formation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expansion of (a + b)^n has coefficients given by the nth row of Pascal's Triangle: each entry is the sum of the two above it; (a + b)^n = sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k) a^{n-k} b^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive derivation: multiply previous expansion by (a+b) and collect like terms; triangular array starting 1,1 and each subsequent row formed by sums yields binomial coefficients. Use the triangular diagram to see the combinatorial coefficients; induction may be used to prove general identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect method (proof by contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement by assuming its negation leads to an impossible conclusion (contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes is a model: assume finitely many primes p1,...,pn; construct A = p1 p2 ... pn + 1 and show contradiction. Indirect proofs are classical and widely used in number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume primes are p1,...,pn; consider A = p1 p2 ... pn + 1. A is larger than any p_i and when divided by any p_i leaves remainder 1, so it cannot be divisible by any known prime; hence assumption of finitely many primes is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be turned into a constructive method: starting from known primes, the product+1 either is a new prime or has prime factors different from the list, so one can build an infinite sequence of primes in principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic (unique prime factorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every integer N > 1 can be expressed as a product of primes in only one way (up to order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by contradiction using the well-ordering principle: assume there exists a smallest integer m with two different prime factorizations m = p1 p2 ... pr = q1 q2 ... qs; rearrange and subtract to derive a smaller counterexample, contradiction. The proof is elementary but subtle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive but fallible prime-generating expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some algebraic expressions produce many primes for small n (e.g., n^2 - n + 41 gives primes for n=1..40) but fail eventually; no simple algebraic formula yields all primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: empirical success for many inputs is not a proof of universality. The search for simple universal prime-generating formulas has been futile; examples demonstrate why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primes in arithmetical progressions (Dirichlet's theorem and special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence suggests each arithmetic progression a, a+d, a+2d, ... with gcd(a,d)=1 contains infinitely many primes; Dirichlet proved this in full generality using advanced analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dirichlet's theorem required powerful analytic tools and is nontrivial. However, some special progressions (e.g., 4n+3, 6n+5) can be handled by elementary Euclid-style modifications (constructing specialized N and analyzing prime factor forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary proof for infinitude of primes in progression 4n+3
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume finitely many primes of form 4n+3: p1,...,pn; consider N = 4(p1 p2 ... pn) - 1 = 4K - 1 (which is of form 4m+3). Any prime divisor of N cannot be among the p_i (it leaves remainder -1) and not all prime divisors can be of form 4n+1, so some prime factor must be of form 4n+3, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses multiplicative closure property of numbers of form 4n+1 and parity of forms to force existence of new 4n+3 prime factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime Number Theorem (asymptotic distribution of primes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A_n be number of primes <= n. Gauss conjectured and Hadamard/de la Vallée Poussin proved that A_n is asymptotically n / log n, i.e., A_n ~ n / log n (equivalently A_n / (n / log n) -> 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: log n is area under hyperbola xy=1 between x=1 and x=n. Empirical tables show A_n/n approximates 1/log n. Proof requires advanced analysis (Riemann, Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mathematical induction and empirical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical induction (a deductive, logical method) is fundamentally different from empirical induction in natural sciences; checking finitely many cases cannot yield a rigorous proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical theorem is only proved when shown to be a necessary logical consequence of accepted assumptions. Empirical verification may suggest conjectures, which then must be proved (often by induction or other deductive means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goldbach's conjecture and partial results
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldbach's conjecture: every even integer (except 2) is the sum of two primes — unproven. Partial results: Schnirelmann proved every positive integer is a sum of <= 800,000 primes (constructive); Vinogradov (and collaborators) reduced bounds and showed every sufficiently large integer is sum of <=4 primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These partial results illustrate differences between constructive and non-constructive proofs: Schnirelmann's is constructive but weak, Vinogradov's is non-constructive and applies only for sufficiently large integers. The difficulty stems from relating multiplicative prime properties to additive problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin prime problem (unsolved)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: primes often occur in pairs p and p+2; whether there are infinitely many such pairs is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a striking open problem with no progress toward a proof at the time of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of congruence modulo d
rubrics_metrics.description: Two integers a and b are congruent modulo d (write a ≡ b (mod d)) if they leave the same remainder on division by d, equivalently a = b + n d for some integer n, equivalently d divides a - b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congruence notation simplifies divisibility reasoning; examples include clock arithmetic (mod 12) and mileage counters mod 100,000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal properties and arithmetic rules of congruences
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruence modulo the same modulus shares equality's properties: reflexive, symmetric, transitive; preserved under addition, subtraction, and multiplication: if a ≡ a' (mod d) and b ≡ b' (mod d) then a+b ≡ a'+b' (mod d), a-b ≡ a'-b' (mod d), ab ≡ a'b' (mod d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: write a = a' + r d, b = b' + s d; algebra shows a+b, a-b, ab differ from a'+b', a'-b', a'b' by multiples of d. These facts make congruences a useful algebraic relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical interpretation of congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: Integers can be represented on a line/segment and congruence classes modulo d correspond to points placed periodically (or positions on a clock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps intuition: congruent numbers are 'the same' with respect to division by d; examples illustrate remainder classes and negative residues.
